paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 10.11 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 10 (Part 4)
paragraphs.text: A lawyer's charges may be reviewed in Alberta (a) at the request of a client if (i) the lawyer resides in Alberta, (ii) the lawyer's principal office is in Alberta, (iii) the lawyer's charges specify an Alberta address for the lawyer or the law firm of the lawyer, (iv) most of the services were performed in Alberta, (v) the services were performed in connection with legal proceedings commenced in Alberta in which the lawyer was a lawyer of record, or (vi) the retainer agreement between the lawyer and the client so provides, and (b) at the request of the lawyer if (i) the client resides in Alberta, (ii) the principal office or place of business of the client is in Alberta, (iii) most of the services were performed in Alberta and the lawyer has no office in the jurisdiction outside Alberta where the client resides or carries on business, or (iv) the retainer agreement between the lawyer and the client so provides.

paragraphs.text: (1) Where a lawyer carries on business in Alberta, the lawyer's charges may be reviewed by a review officer at the judicial centre nearest to where the lawyer carries on business. paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 10.13 – Part 10. Lawyers' Charges, Recoverable Costs Of Litigation, And Sanctions
paragraphs.text: (1) A lawyer or a client may, by request, obtain from a review officer an appointment date for a review of a retainer agreement or a lawyer's charges, or both. (2) If a lawyer obtains an appointment date, the lawyer must file (a) a notice of the appointment in Form 42, (b) a copy of any retainer agreement between the lawyer and the client, and (c) if the appointment is for a review of the lawyer's charges, a copy of a signed account of the lawyer's charges that are to be reviewed. (3) If a client obtains an appointment date, the client must file (a) a notice of the appointment in Form 42, (b) a copy of any retainer agreement between the lawyer and the client, if a copy is available, and (c) if the appointment is for a review of a lawyer's charges, a copy of the lawyer's account that is to be reviewed, if a copy is available. (4) The client or the lawyer who obtains an appointment date for review must serve copies of the documents filed under subrule (2) or (3) on the other party to the review and any other interested party 10 days or more before the appointment date, or within any other period specified by a review officer. (5) A notice of appointment must be filed, endorsed and served in the same manner as a commencement document. Alta. Reg. 140/2013, s. 9; 36/2020, s. 10

paragraphs.text: (1) If a lawyer is served with notice of an appointment for a review of the lawyer's charges or retainer agreement, or both, the lawyer must file (a) a copy of the account, appropriately signed, in respect of which the client seeks a review, (b) a copy of any time records upon which the account is based, and (c) a copy of any retainer agreement between the lawyer and the client whether or not the lawyer intends to rely on them. (2) The documents must be filed 5 days or more before the appointment date or within any other period specified by a review officer, and the review officer may vary the period before or after the time limit has passed. (3) If the lawyer does not comply with this rule, the lawyer forfeits the right to payment of the lawyer's charges in any account that is the subject of a review unless the review officer otherwise directs. paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 10.17 – Part 10. Lawyers' Charges, Recoverable Costs Of Litigation, And Sanctions
paragraphs.text: (1) For the purpose of conducting a review under this Division, a review officer may do all or any of the following: (a) take evidence either by affidavit or orally under oath, or both; (b) direct the production of records; (c) require notice of the appointment for the review to be served on persons who may be affected by the review or who have an interest in the trust, estate, fund or property from which the lawyer's charges are or may be paid or charged; (d) give directions about how notice of the appointment for the review is to be served; (e) allow a party to be represented by a lawyer; (f) require details of a retainer agreement, or of the services provided, money collected and expended, disbursements or other charges claimed or any other matter necessary to understand the agreement or charges and decide whether the agreement or charges, or both, are reasonable; (g) validate service of the notice of the appointment or, if service is impractical or impossible, dispense with service; (h) determine the applicability of a time period specified in these rules in respect of a review conducted under this Division and extend or shorten an applicable time period. (2) A review officer may not review either a retainer agreement or a lawyer's charges that have previously been reviewed by a review officer unless the Court so orders or the parties agree. Alta. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.17:1 Rule 10.17 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.17. Guidelines for Reviewing Contingency Accounts In Sonnenberg v. Schumacher & Associates, 2005 ABQB 352, 2005 CarswellAlta 840, 52 Alta. L.R. (4th) 151, 16 C.P.C. (6th) 88, Germain J. set out the following guidelines for taxing officers who are called upon to review contingency accounts. At pp. 155–156, his Lordship said: I set out the following guidelines for taxing officers to utilize when reviewing contingency accounts. These guidelines are not exhaustive. First, the taxing officer should attempt in a summary way to come to a final decision on the taxation issue, using the referral power only sparingly, unless the client in fact requests the referral as permitted in Rule 619(2). This is consistent with the summary nature of the proceedings, yet protects the interests of the parties, as the issue may still be reviewed de novo by a judge. Second, the taxing officer should review the contingency agreement against the checklist in Rule 616, inviting the lawyer to point out technical compliance, if required. If the taxing officer is not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that technical compliance has occurred, then the taxing officer should advise the lawyer to justify the account on a quantum meruit basis. That is, the lawyer should have the opportunity to prove that the account is fair even without the benefit of the contingency agreement. On the other hand, if the taxing officer is satisfied that the contingency agreement does comply with the Rules, then the taxing officer should conduct the taxation on the basis that the contingency agreement is highly significant to what the taxing officer should consider. The taxing officer should recognize a fundamental entitlement to legal fees on a contingency, but this should not be the only factor for the taxing officer to consider. Third, when taxing an account to which a valid contingency agreement applies, the taxing officer is free to refer to prior cases of comparable complexity. In relatively routine motor vehicle actions, where liability is not greatly in dispute, a contingency of 25% seems to me to be close to the upper limit, absent unusual circumstances. In more complex litigation, such as medical malpractice, even 50% may pass a taxation. There is an economic reality to legal work, such that the law firm may have a sliding scale, which too may pass taxation. The sliding scale may be based on the number of steps taken, with the largest percentage payable in cases that go to trial and a much lower percentage in cases that settle early in the negotiation stage. In the alternative, the sliding scale may have the percentage higher on the first dollars, but lower as the amount collected increases. The taxing officer may find either approach reasonable. It is clear, however, that the taxing officer must do some analysis of the work effort, the risk, and the result, regardless of any valid contingency agreement. Otherwise, Rule 616(2)(h) would be unnecessary. Fourth, in more complicated taxations, the taxing officer may wish to give reasons, but is free not to do so, in light of the summary nature of taxation. Finally, when the taxing officer uses Rule 619(2) to refer a matter to a judge, the taxing officer and the client can expect the judge to deal with all issues arising in the taxation and not only the narrow issue that motivated the referral, although the judge is free not to conduct such a broad review. This is consistent with the summary and expeditious approach to be taken in the taxation of legal accounts. The alternative, of deciding the narrow issue referred and remitting the matter to the taxing officer, should generally be expected only in complex accounts, where there are numerous mathematical calculations and considerations.

The alternative, of deciding the narrow issue referred and remitting the matter to the taxing officer, should generally be expected only in complex accounts, where there are numerous mathematical calculations and considerations.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.18:1 Rule 10.18 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.18. 1. Rules 10.18(1)(a) and 10.9 In Rath & Co. v. Sweetgrass First Nation, 2014 ABCA 426, 2014 CarswellAlta 2278, the Court said commented on the duties of a review officer, and when a reviewing judge may overturn a review officer's decision. At paragraphs 3–6: 3 The reviewing judge correctly noted that the review officer's decision was owed deference unless some improper principle was relied upon, the quantum was so inordinately high or low it revealed a mistaken principle, the review officer failed to consider the evidence and representations, a fact finding was clearly in error, or the review officer exceeded his jurisdiction. As set out in the Alberta Rules of Court, review officers may review retainer agreements and lawyer's charges for reasonableness, but they have no jurisdiction to interpret retainer agreements. Any question arising about the terms of a retainer agreement must be referred to the Court pursuant to Rule 10.18(1)(a). 4 The reviewing judge concluded there was a dispute about the terms of the oral or implied retainer agreements, and therefore the review officer proceeded without jurisdiction because he had to interpret the retainer in order to assess quantum. Mindful that the review officer had stated “In my view, reasonableness is to be read into the clause as follows …” (emphasis added), the reviewing judge held that the review officer exceeded his jurisdiction by improperly interpreting the contingency fee agreement. He further noted that the reductions were prima facie inordinate and raised concerns of principle. 5 In our view, notwithstanding the review officer's choice of words, he did not exceed his jurisdiction. He, in fact, neither interpreted the oral or implied retainer agreements nor the written contingency fee agreement. The record, read as a whole, reveals that he was well aware of the limits on his jurisdiction, and he correctly noted that he was able to review the retainer agreements and the amounts charged for reasonableness only. 6 While some terms of the oral or implied retainer agreements may have been unspecified, that does not mean they must automatically be referred to the court for interpretation. The review officer properly concluded that the accounts could be assessed on a quantum meruit basis because the parties had not expressly agreed beforehand what the fees would be: McDonald Crawford v Morrow, 2004 ABCA 150 at para 11, 348 AR 118. The review officer's comment that reasonableness was to be “read into” the contingency fee agreement does not mean that he was interpreting that agreement. In so doing, he was simply complying with that which Rule 10.9 of the Rules of Court mandates.

paragraphs.text: (1) A review of a lawyer's charges must take into consideration the factors described in rule 10.2, except to the extent that a retainer agreement otherwise provides. (2) A review of a retainer agreement must be based on the circumstances that existed when the retainer agreement was entered into. (3) The review officer may, in a review of a lawyer's charges, allow the charges, or vary, reduce or disallow all or any of the charges, and certify the amount payable for and against each party, and may issue an interim certificate. (4) A review officer's decision must be given by an interim or final certificate, which may be endorsed on a copy of the lawyer's account, and the certificate must (a) certify the amount to be paid by each party or person, (b) certify any special circumstance and the amount to be paid by each party or person with respect to the special circumstance, and (c) be dated and signed by the review officer. (5) An interim or final certificate of a review officer that meets the requirements set out in subrule (4) is conclusive proof of the amount that a party or person who had notice of the review must pay.

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 10.20 – Part 10. Lawyers' Charges, Recoverable Costs Of Litigation, And Sanctions
paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.20:1 Rule 10.20 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.20. 1. Filing Statement of Claim Not Necessary This rule gives the court a discretion to order the enforcement of a solicitor's taxed bill of costs as a judgment of the court. In this respect, I entirely agree with the decision of the master in chambers. Nothing in this rule requires the commencement of an action by way of statement of claim before the granting of an enforcement order. This issue was decided in Griffiths v. Hughes (1847), 16 M. & W. 809 … I have found not subsequent authority to the contrary. Rusnak v. A.C.H.A.I.A. Holdings Ltd. (1983), 28 Alta. L.R. (2d) 187 (Q.B.), at 188, per McFadyen J. 2. Master Has Jurisdiction under Rule There remains to be considered only the issue of whether the exercise of the power conferred by R. 651 is a power reserved to a judge appointed pursuant to s. 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867. To determine this issue, it is necessary to consider the tests set out by Dickson J. in Re Residential Tenancies Act of Ont., [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714 … While the power granted by R. 651(2) may historically have been a power granted to a Superior Court Judge and was a power which was exercised only by a Superior Court Judge at the time of Confederation, I am satisfied that the power now cannot be considered a “judicial function” as that term is defined with Dickson J. at p. 571 where he states: Step two involves consideration of the function within its institutional setting to determine whether the function itself is different when viewed in that setting. In particular, can the function still be considered to be a ‘judicial’ function? In addressing the issue it is important to keep in mind the further statement by Rand J. in Dupont v. Inglis, [1958] S.C.R. 535, 14 D.L.R. (2d) 417 at 424, that ‘it is the subject-matter rather than the apparatus of adjudication that is determinative’. Thus the question of whether any particular function is ‘judicial’ is not to be determined simply on the basis of procedural trappings. The primary issue is the nature of the question which the tribunal is called upon to decide. Where the tribunal is faced with a private dispute between parties, and is called upon to adjudicate through the application of a recognized body of rules in a manner consistent with fairness and impartiality, then, normally, it is acting in a ‘judicial capacity’. To borrow the terminology of Professor Ronald Dworkin, the judicial task involves questions of ‘principle’, that is, consideration of the competing rights of individuals or groups. This can be contrasted with questions of ‘policy’ involving competing views of the collective good of the community as a whole: see Dworkin, Taking Rights Seriously (1977), at pp. 82–90 (Duckworth). In exercising the discretion granted by R. 651(2) the master is not adjudicating on the dispute between two parties or on competing rights or claims of two parties. The function of the master is to ensure that the person against whom the order is sought was in fact served with a notice of taxation and that the certificate of taxation is in the proper form and to ensure that all outstanding issues between the parties have been resolved … It is clear that the taxation certificate is final and conclusive as to amounts mentioned against parties served with the notice of taxation. The rules do not purport to authorize the master to resolve finally and conclusively all issues which may arise between the solicitor and the named defendants respecting the account and the liability to pay that account. Most other issues may be decided on a reference by the taxation officer to the judge of the court. However, where any issues remain unresolved, the application under R. 651(2) should either be rejected and the solicitor left to his remedy to bring an action by way of statement of claim or there should be a direction that the unresolved issue be tried. As a result, I reach the conclusion that the function of the master is not a judicial function as that term is defined by Dickson J. I am satisfied that the master had jurisdiction to deal with the application made pursuant to R. 651(2). Rusnak v. A.C.H.A.I.A. Holdings Ltd. (1983), 28 Alta. L.R. (2d) 187 (Q.B.), at 190–91, per McFadyen J. 3. Prior Determination of Liability Required Where there is a dispute about liability an order under Rule 651(2) is not appropriate until the issue of liability is resolved. That depends on the terms of the agreement, if any, between the client and the solicitors. The application for an order under Rule 651(2) is adjourned pending disposition of the main issue between the parties. Peterson, Ross v. Kirkwood (1984), 52 A.R. 284 (Master), at 293, per Master Funduk, quoting Gilbert v. Douglas Rentals Ltd. (26th July 1983), Edmonton 8303-15325 (Q.B.) (unreported)). In Shreem Holdings Inc. v. Barr Picard, 2013 ABQB 257, 2013 CarswellAlta 540, 560 A.R. 272, 88 Alta. L.R. (5th) 359, 49 C.P.C. (7th) 419, Justice Wakeling said, at paragraphs 25–28, 30–33, and 40: 25 Rule 10.20(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court states that “[t]he Court may direct a decision of a review officer to be entered as a judgment or order”. 26 A judgment is “a decision made by the court upon the respective claims and rights of the parties to a proceeding”. L. Abrams & K. McGuiness, Canadian Civil Procedure Law 1358 (2d ed. 2010). It resolves a dispute and is capable of enforcement. See Bozson v. Altrincham Urban District Council, [1903] 1 K.B. 547, 548 (C.A) (a judgment reflects the final disposition of the “rights of the parties”); 16(2) Halsbury's Law of England 429 (4th ed. reissue (2003) (a judgment in personam determines “the rights of parties as between one another”) & 2 W. Williston & R. Rolls, The Law of Civil Procedure 1020 (1970) (“Decisions which finally determine the … questions at issue in an action inter partes are judgments”. 27 This court should not exercise its discretion in favour of a rule 10.20(1) applicant if the certificate of review, read as a whole, does not resolve a dispute between a client and a lawyer. 28 No purpose is served by giving a certificate of review the status of a judgment when it can never be enforced. That is the sole rationale of rule 10.20(1). See Griffith v. Hughes, 153 E.R. 1418 (Ex. 1847). … 30 A review officer who conducts a review of a lawyer's charges has a limited jurisdiction under the Alberta Rules of Court. This is the case with respect to both procedural and substantive matters. 31 Significant substantive limitations restrict the questions the review officer may resolve. According to rule 10.19(3) of the Alberta Rules of Court, a review officer “may … allow the [lawyer] charges, or vary, reduce or disallow all or any of the charges and certify the amount payable for and against each party”. The rules even dictate the factors the review officer must take into account in arriving at a reasonable charge. Alberta Rules of Court, rule 10.19(1). 32 A review officer may not make any substantive decision not listed in rule 10.19(3). 33 It follows that a review officer may not determine if a solicitor-client relationship exists. Gilbert v. Douglas Rentals Ltd., [1983] A.J. No. 664, Edmonton Q.B. 8303-15325 (Master July 26, 1983) (“Like any other contract a dispute about the terms must be resolved by a judicial officer”). Nor may the review officer adjudicate a claim that the lawyer agreed to accept a fixed fee. Rusnak v. Commodity Investors Syndicate of Canada Ltd., 48 A.R. 311, 315 (Q. B 1982) (a taxing officer could not hear client's claim that the lawyer had agreed to a fixed fee). The review officer is also sailing in prohibited water if he settles the amount a client had paid towards an account. … 40 A court should not accord the status of a judgment to a review officer's certificate of review which reveals that there is a dispute as to who the client is and the amount the client owes the lawyer. Gibson v. Bassie, Kantor & Plupek[1985] 2 A.U.D. 923, 924 (C.A.) (a court may enforce a taxation certificate “as a judgment … unless the terms of the retainer are disputed”); Rusnak and Savaryn v. A.C.H.A.I.A. Holdings Ltd., 51 A.R. 196, 201 (Q.B. 1983) (a taxation certificate should not be entered by court order as a judgment “where a substantial issue exists as to the liability of the defendant or any one of them”); Peterson, Ross v. Kirwood, 52 A.R. 284, 292 (Master 1984) (“As the taxing officer has no jurisdiction to decide liability it would be illogical to hold his certificate prevents a client … from disputing liability); Field and Field v. Hys, 101 A.R. 31, 34 (Master 1989) (taxation certificate not enforced because alleged clients denied they were responsible for the account); Brian A. Beresh Professional Corporation v. Schneider, 106 A.R. 251, 293 (Master 1990) (taxation certificate not enforced as if it were a judgment because the husband denied he was responsible for his wife's legal fees); Gilbert v. Douglas Rentals Ltd., Edmonton Q.B. 8303-15325 (Master July 26, 1983) (“where there is a dispute about liability an order under Rule 651(2) is not appropriate until the issue of liability is resolved”) &Rusnak v. Commodity Investors Syndicate of Canada Ltd., 48 A.R. 311, 315–16 (Q.B 1982) (the court refused to enforce a taxing officer's assessment because there was a dispute about the existence of a fixed fee). 4. Client May Obtain Judgment for Overpayment In Welsh v. Jones (1998), 60 Alta. L.R. (3d) 331 (Master), a lawyer rendered an account for professional services, and it was paid by the client. However, the client taxed the account and it was reduced by $1,800. The lawyer did not repay the overpayment. The client applied to have the overpayment enforced against the lawyer (who had subsequently left the practice of law). In allowing the client's application, Master Alberstat, at p. 332, said: The rule under which lawyers apply to have their taxed bills enforced as judgments seems to apply only to lawyers taxing a bill. In any event that is how it has been interpreted and treated by practise [sic] and usage. The question is whether a client can avail him or herself of the same rule? Rule 4 says: As to all matters not provided for in the Rules the practice as far as may be shall be regulated by analogy thereto. The respondent argues that there is a provision provided for by [sic] the client and that is to sue for the amount taxed down. I reject that argument. A lawyer may tax a bill either before or after payment although usually the taxation is prior to payment. A client may tax a bill of a lawyer either before or after payment. If the bill is taxed prior to payment the lawyer may then apply under rule 651, to have the taxation enforced as a judgment. If a bill is taxed after it is paid, and is taxed down, the payment is an overpayment. The person having made the payment is entitled to be repaid the amount overpaid. If a lawyer can have an unpaid taxed bill enforced as a judgment pursuant to rule 651 then why can not a client have the overpayment enforced as a judgment? I cannot see why that should not be the case applying rule 4.

26 A judgment is “a decision made by the court upon the respective claims and rights of the parties to a proceeding”.
L.
Abrams & K.
McGuiness, Canadian Civil Procedure Law 1358 (2d ed.
It resolves a dispute and is capable of enforcement.
See Bozson v.
Altrincham Urban District Council, [1903] 1 K.B.

547, 548 (C.A) (a judgment reflects the final disposition of the “rights of the parties”); 16(2) Halsbury's Law of England 429 (4th ed. reissue (2003) (a judgment in personam determines “the rights of parties as between one another”) & 2 W.
Williston & R.
Rolls, The Law of Civil Procedure 1020 (1970) (“Decisions which finally determine the … questions at issue in an action inter partes are judgments”.
27 This court should not exercise its discretion in favour of a rule 10.20(1) applicant if the certificate of review, read as a whole, does not resolve a dispute between a client and a lawyer.
28 No purpose is served by giving a certificate of review the status of a judgment when it can never be enforced.
That is the sole rationale of rule 10.20(1).
See Griffith v.
Hughes, 153 E.R.
1847). … 30 A review officer who conducts a review of a lawyer's charges has a limited jurisdiction under the Alberta Rules of Court.
This is the case with respect to both procedural and substantive matters.
31 Significant substantive limitations restrict the questions the review officer may resolve.

According to rule 10.19(3) of the Alberta Rules of Court, a review officer “may … allow the [lawyer] charges, or vary, reduce or disallow all or any of the charges and certify the amount payable for and against each party”.
The rules even dictate the factors the review officer must take into account in arriving at a reasonable charge.
Alberta Rules of Court, rule 10.19(1).
32 A review officer may not make any substantive decision not listed in rule 10.19(3).

No.
664, Edmonton Q.B.
8303-15325 (Master July 26, 1983) (“Like any other contract a dispute about the terms must be resolved by a judicial officer”).

Holdings Ltd., 51 A.R.
1983) (a taxation certificate should not be entered by court order as a judgment “where a substantial issue exists as to the liability of the defendant or any one of them”); Peterson, Ross v.

284, 292 (Master 1984) (“As the taxing officer has no jurisdiction to decide liability it would be illogical to hold his certificate prevents a client … from disputing liability); Field and Field v.

31, 34 (Master 1989) (taxation certificate not enforced because alleged clients denied they were responsible for the account); Brian A.
Beresh Professional Corporation v.
Schneider, 106 A.R.
251, 293 (Master 1990) (taxation certificate not enforced as if it were a judgment because the husband denied he was responsible for his wife's legal fees); Gilbert v.

Jones (1998), 60 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 331 (Master), a lawyer rendered an account for professional services, and it was paid by the client.

The lawyer did not repay the overpayment.
The client applied to have the overpayment enforced against the lawyer (who had subsequently left the practice of law).
In allowing the client's application, Master Alberstat, at p.
332, said: The rule under which lawyers apply to have their taxed bills enforced as judgments seems to apply only to lawyers taxing a bill.
In any event that is how it has been interpreted and treated by practise [sic] and usage.
The question is whether a client can avail him or herself of the same rule?
Rule 4 says: As to all matters not provided for in the Rules the practice as far as may be shall be regulated by analogy thereto.

A lawyer may tax a bill either before or after payment although usually the taxation is prior to payment.
A client may tax a bill of a lawyer either before or after payment.
If the bill is taxed prior to payment the lawyer may then apply under rule 651, to have the taxation enforced as a judgment.
If a bill is taxed after it is paid, and is taxed down, the payment is an overpayment.
The person having made the payment is entitled to be repaid the amount overpaid.
If a lawyer can have an unpaid taxed bill enforced as a judgment pursuant to rule 651 then why can not a client have the overpayment enforced as a judgment?
I cannot see why that should not be the case applying rule 4.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.22:1 Rule 10.22—Action for costs due See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.22. 1. Purpose Although the rule [then R. 626] is rather unhappily worded, it has been generally interpreted in the Court of Queen's Bench as referring to actions brought by lawyers to recover legal fees. The rule, for reasons of public policy, prohibits a solicitor from obtaining judgment in Queen's Bench for his legal account by default without a court order … Because a solicitor is an officer of the court, the Court of Queen's Bench and the courts which preceded it have never allowed a solicitor to obtain a judgment for his legal fees against a client, even one who is in default, without being satisfied that the account is fair and reasonable (see R. 613). After examining a lawyer's account a Queen's Bench judge either orders the bill taxed or dispenses with a taxation as he sees fit. It has never been the practice in the Court of Queen's Bench to insist that a solicitor have his account taxed in every instance before judgment is entered. The application of R. 626 was discussed by Cavanagh J. in Fowle, Todd & Co. v. Klassen (1980), 31 A.R. 494 at 496 (Q.B.): It is true that not every account need be taxed. However, a judge cannot dispense with taxation of an account he has never seen. It seems to me elementary that a copy of the account should accompany an application to enter judgment. Furthermore, I think the very least the solicitor can do is to prepare his bill showing all the detail required under R. 645. One significant consideration in deciding whether a solicitor's account should be taxed has always been the amount of the account. The smaller the legal bill the less likely Queen's Bench will require a taxation with its attendant delay and expense to the parties … Referring again to R. 626, it is important to note that the rule is directed to the clerk of the Court of Queen's Bench. The purpose of the rule is to prohibit the clerk from entering judgment by default when a solicitor has sued for legal fees. It creates an exception to the main rule which permits the clerk to enter a default judgment in a case involving a claim for a debt or liquidated demand upon the claimant satisfying the clerk that proper service has been made and that the defendant has not filed a statement of defence or demand of notice. Dennis W. Crowe Professional Corp. v. Allford (1983), 26 Alta. L.R. (2d) 21 (Q.B.), at 24–25, per Holmes J. 2. Application of Rule There are conflicting Provincial Court decisions about whether then Rule 626 applies to actions brought in the Provincial Court. In Murska Management (1969) Ltd. v. Flesher (1990), 118 A.R. 251 (Prov. Ct.), His Honour Judge Allford said at p. 253: I see no real distinction between a barrister and solicitor getting a default judgment and any other claimant other than the obstruction afforded in rule 626. But where you look at [s. 53(1) of the Provincial Court Act] which does … set out a mandatory provision that the Clerk of the court shall enter a default judgment once the preliminaries that are mentioned … in the section are met, that, in my view, would override the application of 626. However, in Witten LLP v. Arsenault, 2006 ABPC 29, 2006 CarswellAlta 132, 393 A.R. 216, 27 C.P.C. (6th) 174, Judge Ingram specifically disagreed, and said, at paras. 29–32: In my view, Rule 626 should apply to all accounts between lawyers and their clients both in the Court of Queen's Bench and the Provincial Court. At the present time, a serious anomaly exists. Under the Murska Management (1969) Ltd. judgment and the practice of the Provincial Court, a solicitor's account may be treated as a debt or liquidated demand in respect of which a default judgment may be entered without any supervision from the court.30 In this respect, I concur entirely with the observations of Holmes, J., in Dennis W. Crowe Professional Corp. v. Allford, supra, as follows: ¶ 8 Although [Rule 626] is rather unhappily worded, it has been generally interpreted in the Court of Queen's Bench as referring to actions brought by lawyers to recover legal fees. The rule, for reasons of public policy, prohibits a solicitor from obtaining judgment in Queen's Bench for his legal account by default without a court order. It was argued that unless the rule is applied in the Small Claims Division solicitors will not only effectively by-pass a long standing public policy requirement by obtaining a judgment by default in Provincial Court but will do so without being required to tax their accounts. ¶ 9 Because a solicitor is an officer of the court, the Court of Queen's Bench and the courts which preceded it have never allowed a solicitor to obtain a judgment for his legal fees against a client, even one who is in default, without being satisfied that the account is fair and reasonable (see Rule 613). After examining a lawyer's account a Queen's Bench judge either orders the bill taxed or dispenses with a taxation as he sees fit. It has never been the practice in the Court of Queen's Bench to insist that a solicitor have his account taxed in every instance before judgment is entered. ¶ 10 The application of Rule 626 was discussed by Cavanagh, J., in Fowle, Todd & Co. v. Klassen (1980), 31 A.R. 494 at 496 (Q.B.): It is true that not every account need be taxed. However, a judge cannot dispense with taxation of an account he has never seen. It seems to me elementary that a copy of the account should accompany an application to enter judgment. Furthermore, I think the very least the solicitor can do is to prepare his bill showing all the detail required under Rule 645. One significant consideration in deciding whether a solicitor's account should be taxed has always been the amount of the account. The smaller the legal bill the less likely Queen's Bench will require a taxation with its attendant delay and expense to the parties. The public policy which is the basis of Rule 626 should be the same in Provincial Court as in the Court of Queen's Bench and is the same now as it was in 1983. No legislative or regulatory change is required to achieve harmonious application of the law in the Provincial and the Queen's Bench courts in accordance with principle of public policy that prevents a lawyer from obtaining default judgment for his legal account without a court order. The Provincial Court should simply apply Rule 626 and require a court order prior to judgment in all actions for lawyer's accounts. The Provincial Court Judge to whom an action for a lawyer's account is referred, must then examine the account and either “order the account taxed or dispense with taxation as he sees fit”. As Holmes, J., points out it is not the practice to insist that the account be taxed in every instance before judgment is entered. The adoption of the practice outlined above is necessary to ensure consistency in the practices of the two courts with concurrent jurisdiction, a matter of some legitimate concern since the increase in the monetary jurisdiction of the Provincial Court. As I indicated earlier, Taxation (within its scope) may be preferred over assessment of legal fees by individual Provincial Court judges in some cases and should not be precluded nor, of course, should it be used where not appropriate.

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 10.24 – Part 10. Lawyers' Charges, Recoverable Costs Of Litigation, And Sanctions
paragraphs.text: (1) If any of the following events occurs, a lawyer, the lawyer's personal representative or a client may make an appointment with a review officer for the purpose of determining the amount of the lawyer's charges payable by the client: (a) the lawyer dies; (b) the lawyer is suspended, disbarred or incapacitated; (c) the lawyer ceases to be the client's lawyer or the client ceases to be the lawyer's client; (d) a dispute arises about the apportionment of contingency fees under a contingency fee agreement under which 2 or more lawyers are engaged, whether or not the contingency has occurred; (e) the client retains a new lawyer in the action; (f) the client unreasonably discontinues or abandons any matter to which a contingency fee agreement applies; (g) any other event that creates uncertainty about a lawyer's charges or who is to pay them or to whom they are to be paid. (2) When making a decision under this rule, the review officer must take into consideration the factors described in rule 10.2, except to the extent that a retainer agreement otherwise provides.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.24:1 Rule 10.24 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.24. In Lising v. Smith, 2018 ABQB 1061, 2018 CarswellAlta 3189, Justice Shelley had before her an appeal by a lawyer from a Review Officer's decision in relation to a retainer agreement between the lawyer and his then client. The lawyer submitted that the “Review Officer ought not to have reviewed his [the lawyer's] account because more than six months had passed between the date [the lawyer] sent the account [to the client] and the date the Appointment for Review was filed.” Justice Shelley found that the lawyer “did not complete the services contemplated in the Retainer Agreement. He was suspended [by the Law Society], the result of which is that he ceased to be capable of completing the services because he could no longer be the Respondents' lawyer.” Justice Shelley found that Rule 10.24 applied, that Rule 10.24 was not subject to the time limitation set out in Rule 10.10(2). Her Ladyship said: [21]… More importantly, Rule 10.24 is a separate Rule specific to this circumstance and does not contain any limitation on a client's right to have a lawyer's charges reviewed where, for any of the reasons set out in that Rule, a lawyer is unable to complete the services for which the lawyer was retained. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 10.27:1 Rule 10.27 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.27. 1. Nature of Hearing The appeal is not a hearing de novo. The majority of Canadian authorities support the conclusion that on an appeal from a taxing officer “the judicial approach appears rather uniform and is one of non-interference unless the taxing master operated on a wrong principle and thereby fell into error”. This statement is taken from a judgment of the Nova Scotia Supreme Court Appeal Division in Cape Breton Landowners v. Stora Kopparbergs Bergslags Aktiebolag (1983), 33 C.P.C. 1 … The relevant Nova Scotia rule is in the same terms as R. 657. A number of other authorities are review in that decision. If the quantum awarded can be said to be inordinately high or low, that is a ground of interference because it betrays an error of principle. Once error is found the reviewing court may then make its own assessment. The solicitors cite Carter v. Blake (1982), 41 A.R. 418 (N.W.T.C.A.), where the comparable rule in the Northwest Territories was under consideration. McClung J.A. speaks of the “de novo” aspect of the proceedings before him. That case acknowledges that the judge hearing the appeal from a taxation may review a finding of fact that is clearly in error, although McClung J.A. upheld the taxing officer's fact finding. The case does not decide whether the proceeding before the judge hearing an appeal from a taxing officer is de novo but it reaffirms the rule that fact findings by a taxing officer “should be treated with the same consideration and on the same footing as those made by a trial Judge”, citing Re Solicitor (1976), 3 C.P.C. 148 at 151 (Ont. C.A.) … The solicitors' case is based on the assumption that the calculation of the proper amount of fees is, itself, a matter of discretion. While we do find that term used from time to time, I prefer the view that the assessment is not “the exercise of a discretion”. It is a determination of value or worth which ordinarily involves a weighing of the factors relevant to that assessment like any determination of a quantum meruit claim. I do not read R. 657 as giving the judge sitting on appeal a power to reassess or reweigh the material before the taxing officer. There are some matters of discretion open to a taxing officer and open for review by the judge hearing the appeal, but not the assessment of a value. In making his assessment the taxing officer is not exercising a discretion, any more than the judge who fixes general damages is exercising a discretion. There are practical grounds for not making the hearing before the reviewing judge a de novo hearing. In the first place, the taxing officer will often hear evidence and examine material which gives rise to questions of credit or weight. A chambers judge cannot effectively substitute his views on such questions. Moreover, the taxing officer's function is a specialized one and he may have to bring his own experience and expertise to bear. It is thus unlikely that the standard of review should be “de novo”. In my view in Alberta the primary question on review of a quantum fixed by a taxing officer is (as in many other jurisdictions) whether he has made an error of principle, or whether the award is inordinately high or low. McLennan Ross v. Mercantile Bank of Canada (1988), 59 Alta. L.R. (2d) 369 at 370–72 (C.A.). In Brown v. Snyder & Associates (2004), 364 A.R. 266 (Q.B.), Acton J. said (at pp. 270–271): In 509703 Alberta Ltd. v. Witten Binder, 2000 ABQB 729, Chief Justice Wachowich held that pursuant to Rule 656, the appeal of the decision of a taxing officer is generally not a hearing de novo but a true appeal in which the decision is entitled to curial deference unless there has been an error of principle, an error of law, or the award is so inordinately high or low as to indicate an error of principle or law (at para. 11). 2. Standard of Review The reasons of the taxing officer were, in our view, adequate. This is not to say that his judgment cannot be questioned. The correct standard of review in the circumstances to apply in circumstances of this case is whether the award of the taxing officer was so inordinately high or low as to require interference; the learned chambers judge did not apply that standard, and his decision cannot be left to stand. McLennan Ross v. Keen Industries Ltd. (1987), 55 Alta. L.R. (2d) 290 at 292 (C.A.). In Condominium Plan No. 911945 v. Zavislake (1998), 215 A.R. 355 (Q.B.), Shannon J. said, at p. 357: On appeal, the Chambers judge has a high standard of review. He or she may not substitute his or her opinion for that of the taxation officer, unless the award appears inordinately high or low, indicating an error of principle. And Jones J. said at p. 333 of Carr & Co. v. Markdale Ltd. (1996), 46 Alta. L.R. (3d) 324 (Q.B.): It is clear from what the Court of Appeal had to say in the McLennan Ross cases that the Taxing Officer's decision can only be reversed if it is indicative of error in legal approach. That error would likely appear only in one of two circumstances, namely, from either an enunciation of the application of a principle that would appear to be in error, or from the Taxing Officer having made an award that is either so inordinately high or so inordinately low that the Court must apprehend from the nature of the award that a wrong principle was applied. The only other consideration that could have a bearing on matters would be whether the Taxing Officer had in fact considered the evidence and representations made before the officer. In Carr & Co. v. Markdale Ltd., Mr. Justice Jones noted that Taxing Officers acquire an expertise the benefits of which ought not to be lightly disregarded. At pp. 333–34, his Lordship said: It should be noted that in the [Petty v. Bishop (1977), 2 A.R. 241] case … Miller, J., at p. 244 … quotes from Frost v. Frost, [1941] 3 W.W.R. 273 (B.C. C.A.) at 274 where McDonald, J.A. said: The rule that a judge should not override a registrar (in matters of costs) except on a matter of principle has never been due to any jurisdictional restriction; it is simply a rule of policy and good sense, adopted because registrars can go into details better than can judges. That is a major consideration in this case. I have had the benefit of looking at the detailed accounts prepared and submitted by Carr & Company to the Taxing Officer. I have read them and thought about them. I am nevertheless at a disadvantage compared with the Taxing Officer whose duties commonly call for him to do this type of vetting because of the nature of his position and the expertise that he gathers in carrying out those duties. Accordingly, I am not in a position to say, in the absence of any indication, that he followed a wrong principle or failed to follow an applicable principle, that he has erred in principle by the assessment which he has carried out. Certainly, his enunciation of the various considerations that should go into consideration of the appropriateness of such fees is comprehensive and, in my respectful view, correct. Nor can I conclude, in the circumstances of this case, that the reduction of $11,000, which he ordered, results in an award so inordinately low that it is reflective of the application of a wrong principle or principles. Some deference is due to his determination because of his expertise and experience in this field. In Brown v. Snyder & Associates (2004), 364 A.R. 266 (Q.B.), Acton J. said (at p. 271): Panther Petroleum Ltd. v. Code Hunter, [2002] A.R. Uned. 232, 2002 ABQB 158, sets out the standard for review of an appeal from a decision of a taxing officer. In that case, Justice Rooke canvasses the law on appeals from taxation and notes that according to the Court of Appeal, the appropriate question is whether the Taxing Officer has made an error of principle. The Court sitting on appeal of a taxation is not to re-tax unless that becomes necessary because the Taxing Officer has made an error; for example, on the issue of the scope of the retainer. In Panther Petroleum, Justice Rooke also quotes from Stevenson, J.A., in McLennan Ross v. Keen Industries Ltd. (No. 2) (1988), 86 A.R. 311 (C.A), where Mr. Justice Stevenson states (at para. 11): I do not read Rule 657 as giving the judge sitting on appeal a power to re-assess or re-weigh the material before the taxing officer. There are some matters of discretion open to a taxing officer and open for review by the judge hearing the appeal, but not the assessment of a value. In making his assessment, the taxing officer is not exercising a discretion any more than the judge who fixes general damages is exercising a discretion. In my view, this Court sitting on appeal should not interfere with a finding of credibility unless there is a clear error of principle or law. Finally, Acton J. noted (at pp. 271–272) that “the case law is clear that taxing officers are not required to give extensive reasons …. a complete lack of reasons may be grounds to refer a matter back to the taxing officer…” In Repchuk v. Silverberg, 2013 ABQB 305, Justice Tilleman set out the law relating to reviewing officers and appeals from their decisions. At paragraphs 38, 42–46, 51, 53–55, 57, 58, 63–66, 77–79, his Lordship said: 38 A review officer may fall into error in at least the following ways: 1. erring in fact, for which a party must demonstrate that the fact as found is “clearly in error”: Sweetgrass First Nation v. Rath & Company, 2013 ABQB 165 at para 27 [Rath & Co], FMC v. Kristof Financial Inc, 2012 ABQB 359 at para 17, 215 ACWS (3d) 1010 [FMC], McLennan Ross v. Keen Industries Ltd (No 2) (1988), 86 AR 311 at para 7 (CA) [McLennan Ross 2]; 2. erring in principle (law), which will be shown if a party can demonstrate that the review officer proceeded on an erroneous principle, failed to apply a required principle or that the award of the review officer is so high or low as to betray an error of principle: Rath & Co at para 27, McLennan Ross 2 at paras 6, 13; 3. erring in true questions of jurisdiction (law), for which a standard of correctness will apply: Rath & Co at para 20, Panther Petroleum Ltd v. Code Hunter, 2002 ABQB 158 at para 16, 112 ACWS (3d) 225, MacKimmie Matthews v. Hector (1998), 219 AR 163 at para 7 (CA); and 4. failing to provide a hearing that is procedurally fair, for which a standard of correctness will apply: Anderson v. Alberta Securities Commission, 2008 ABCA 184 at para 30, 437 AR 55 [Anderson]. … 42 A review officer adjudicates the “rights, privileges or interests of an individual” not in a legislative context and owes at least some duty of procedural fairness to the parties in a review hearing: Cardinal v. Director of Kent Institution, [1985] 2 SCR 643 at 653; see also Nicholson v. Haldimand-Norfolk Regional Board of Commissioners of Police, [1979] 1 SCR 311 at 324 and Canada (Attorney General) v. Mavi, 2011 SCC 30 at para 38, [2011] 2 SCR 504. 43 The true question is not whether the procedure must be fair, but what must be done so that the procedure is fair in the context of review proceedings. Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 SCR 817 [Baker] is the seminal case in this regard. A review of the factors in Baker indicates that while review proceedings are important, they will not attract the most stringent of procedural protections. Baker at para 22 is a reminder to: ensure that administrative decisions are made using a fair and open procedure, appropriate to the decision being made and its statutory, institutional, and social context, with an opportunity for those affected by the decision to put forward their views and evidence fully and have them considered by the decision-maker. 44 Review hearings are meant to be an expedited process which confirms for clients the reasonableness of fees and for lawyers allows expedited collection of unpaid accounts: Twinn v. Sawridge Band, 2012 ABQB 44 at paras 36–37, 531 AR 158 [Twinn]. While it is important that decisions be fair, and efficient, finality also play a significant role in advancing the goals of review proceedings. The content of the duty of fairness will also reflect the reality that, because of the nature of review proceedings, additional procedural protections are squared up against decisions made in a necessarily subjective area. 45 Ensuring a minimum standard of procedural fairness is reviewable on a correctness standard: Anderson at para 30. … 46 It is important that a person whose case is decided by a review officer has “a meaningful opportunity to present their case fully and fairly”: Baker at para 30 … … 51 … A review officer must consider the submissions of the parties at a review hearing: Carr & Co v. Markdale Ltd (1996), 197 AR 6 at para 17 (QB). … 53 Where reasons are required, they should demonstrate “justification, transparency and intelligibility” in the decision-making process: Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses' Union v. Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62 at para 1, [2011] 3 SCR 708 [Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses' Union]. 54 A review officer is an expert decision maker and is presumed to know the principles applicable to a review proceeding. Therefore, a review officer's reasons need not be extensive. In Brown v. Snyder & Associates, 2004 ABQB 899 at para 25, 364 A.R. 266, Acton J stated: [T]he case law is clear that taxing officers are not required to give extensive reasons … While a complete lack of reasons may be grounds to refer a matter back to the taxing officer, as found in Penonzek v. Cerra, 2001 ABQB 272, any deficiencies in the articulation of the Taxing Officer's reasons in this case are not a sufficient basis for me to interfere with his decision. [Citations omitted.] 55 Because of their nature, review awards are perhaps subject to the appearance of arbitrariness, although they may not actually be arbitrary or unfair. The British Columbia Court of Appeal in Pamela S Boles Law Corp v. Mathisen (1998), 19 CPC (4th) 78 at para 22, 79 ACWS (3d) 168 accepted “an element of arbitrariness” in the reviewed account because reviewing a lawyer's bill “is an assessment, not merely a mathematical exercise.” … 57 With reference to Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses' Union, the Alberta Court of Appeal recently wrote about the adequacy of reasons in Lameman v. Alberta, 2013 ABCA 148 at para 57: In Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses' Union v. Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62 at para 12, [2011] 3 SCR 708, the Supreme Court of Canada stated that a reviewing court is entitled to consider what reasons a decision-maker could have given. So long as her reasoning path is evident, her reasons are adequate to inform the litigant and are capable of adequate appellate review: para 16. See also R. v. REM, 2008 SCC 51 at paras 24–25, [2008] 3 SCR 3. 58 Attention should also be drawn to Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses' Union at para 12, where the Supreme Court of Canada emphasizes that, before finding reasons inadequate, the Court should seek to supplement reasons with those reasons which could have been offered in support of a decision. … 63 Review officers cannot interpret retainer agreements. I recently determined in Rath & Co at paras 37–38 that: [t]he interplay between rules 10.18(1)(a) and 10.9 works as follows. First, the retainer agreement must be understood. Either its meaning is clear on its face or the parties may agree in front of the review officer as to the meaning; however, if there are doubts about the interpretation, the Court must ascertain its meaning. Thus, when the retainer agreement is properly understood, the review officer may consider if the retainer agreement is reasonable. However, when a review officer faces the need to resolve a “question arising about the terms of a retainer agreement”, rule 10.18(1)(a) requires a court reference. See also the cases cited therein. 64 The Ontario Court of Appeal has recently confirmed, in Cookish v Paul Lee Associates Professional Corp, 2013 ONCA 278, (para 20) that: … an assessment officer [the equivalent of a review officer] has no jurisdiction to determine disputes relating to the existence, nature, terms or extent of a retainer agreement where the order is obtained on requisition [a process initiated by the parties]. There are only two exceptions to this proposition: (i) where there is really no legitimate dispute regarding the retainer; or (ii) where the dispute relates only to the quantum of the bill …[Emphasis added] This reflects the law in Alberta; where the meaning of a clause in a retainer agreement is clear on its face, there is no legitimate dispute about interpretation. 65 It is important to emphasize that the jurisdictional limit which prevents a review officer from interpreting a retainer agreement does not mean that every time a retainer agreement exists the review officer must make a court reference. That is not what the Rules intend and, indeed, would undermine the ability for a review to be a “faster, less expensive alternative” to filing a statement of claim: Twinn at para 37. 66 As discussed in Rath & Co, a review officer need not refer to this Court a question on the interpretation of a retainer agreement where the meaning of the retainer agreement is clear on its face or the parties agree on its meaning. … Whether the Review Officer erred in principle 77 The traditional formulation is that an error in principle is proven by directly showing an error in principle or proving that the award is so high or low as to betray an error of principle: McLennan Ross 2 at paras 6, 13. Accordingly, absent direct evidence on the record showing that a review officer applied an incorrect principle or was ignorant to a required principle, a review officer will be afforded significant deference. … 78 There are a wide variety of factors that a review officer should consider when reviewing a lawyer's account. Rule 10.2 provides direction on the relevant factors to apply, which has been confirmed by the Courts: Rath & Co at para 76, McDonald Crawford v. Morrow, 2004 ABCA 150 at para 11, 348 AR 118. That rule lists a number of factors including “any other factor that is appropriate to consider in the circumstances.” Case law and the Law Society of Alberta, Code of Conduct [Code of Conduct] are sources that help identify other potentially relevant factors. 79 Factors potentially relevant to an assessment of quantum include: Rule 10.2(1) factors include: the nature, importance and urgency of the matter; the client's circumstances; the trust, estate or fund, if any, out of which the lawyer's charges are to be paid; the manner in which the services are performed; and the skill, work and responsibility involved. Common law factors include: the difficulty of the matter; the monetary value at stake; the competence of the lawyer; the results achieved; the client's expectations regarding fees; the client's ability to pay; the solicitor's bill, which is the solicitor's conscientious estimate of the value of the work performed; and an agreement between lawyer and client: Rath & Co at para 77, MacDonald & Freund v. Chernetski (1987), 81 AR 142 at paras 21–26, 29–46 (QB), 509703 Alberta Ltd v. Witten Binder, 2000 ABQB 729 at paras 27–30, McLennan Ross 1 at para 9; Morrison v. Pantony (Rod) Professional Corp, 2008 ABCA 145 at para 26, 429 AR 259 [Rod Pantony Corp] Code of Conduct r 2.06(1) commentary factors (excluding those already listed) include: the time and effort required and spent; any special skill or service that has been required and provided; fees authorized by statute or regulation; special circumstances; the likelihood, if made known to the client, that acceptance of the retainer will result in the lawyer's inability to accept other employment; the experience and ability of the lawyer; any estimate or range of fees given by the lawyer; and the client's prior consent to the fee. Repchuk v. Silverberg, 2013 ABQB 305, was referred to with approval in Ashraf v. Zinner Law Office, 2013 ABQB 730, 2013 CarswellAlta 2546, 578 A.R. 334, 56 C.P.C. (7th) 145. In Fraser Milner Casgrain LLP v. Kristof Financial Inc., 2012 ABQB 359, 2012 CarswellAlta 954, 541 A.R. 245, Justice Yamauchi said, at paragraphs 16–18: 16 When one reviews the many cases that deal with appeals from decisions of review officers (or taxing officers, as they were formerly known), there are certain principles that emerge. A review officer's decision is entitled to curial deference: 509703 at para 11. Why? A review officer's “duties commonly call for him to do this type of vetting because of the nature of his position and the expertise that he gathers in carrying out those duties”: Carr & Co v. Markdale Ltd. (1996), 46 Alta LR (3d) 324 at para 20 (QB) [“Carr & Company”]. See also McLennan Ross v. Mercantile Bank of Canada (1988), 59 Alta LR (2d) 369 at para 6 (CA) [“McLennan Ross”]. The Alberta Court of Appeal in McLennan Ross went on to say that, “the taxing officer's function is a specialized one and he may have to bring his own experience and expertise to bear” (at para 12). 17 Curial deference, however, is not absolute. A court hearing an appeal from a review officer's decision may interfere if the review officer “operated on a wrong principle and thereby fell into error”: McLennan Ross at para 6, citing Cape Breton Landowners v. Stora Kopparbergs Bergslags Aktiebolag (1983), 33 CPC 1, 146 DLR (3d) 369, 58 NSR (2d) 193, 123 APR (NSCA); Petty v. Bishop & McKenzie (1977), 2 AR 241 at 243 (QB). An error in principle may include a situation where the quantum that the review officer awards is inordinately high or low: McLennan Ross ibid; 509703 at para 11. Similarly, a court hearing an appeal from a review officer's decision may interfere if the review officer makes an error concerning the scope of the retainer agreement under which the parties are operating: Brown v. Snyder & Associates, 2004 ABQB 899 at para 20 [“Brown”]. Finally, a court hearing an appeal from a review officer's decision may find that the review officer made a finding of fact that is clearly in error: Carter v. Blake (1982), 41 AR 418 at para 7 (NWTCA) [“Carter”]. 18 With respect to the latter point, a court hearing an appeal from a review officer's decision must exercise caution, and must not step too far into arena of gathering evidence and weighing that evidence. As the court said in McLennan Ross at paras 11–12: I do not read R. 657 as giving the judge sitting on appeal a power to reassess or reweigh the material before the taxing officer. There are some matters of discretion open to a taxing officer and open for review by the judge hearing the appeal, but not the assessment of a value. In making his assessment the taxing officer is not exercising a discretion, any more than the judge who fixes general damages is exercising a discretion. There are practical grounds for not making the hearing before the reviewing judge a de novo hearing. In the first place, the taxing officer will often hear evidence and examine material which gives rise to questions of credit or weight. A chambers judge cannot effectively substitute his views on such questions. This makes it clear that the parties must put forward their “best case” to the review officer; not to the court hearing the appeal. In Ashraf v. Zinner Law Office, 2013 ABQB 730, 2013 CarswellAlta 2546, 578 A.R. 334, 56 C.P.C. (7th) 145, Justice Sullivan referred with approval to those statements by Justice Yamauchi's, and added this comment (at paragraph 29): 29 Additionally, a review officer's decision may be interfered with if the review officer failed to consider the parties' evidence and representations made on the review: Sweetgrass First Nation v. Rath & Company, 2013 ABQB 165 at para 27 [Rath]; Markdale Ltd v. Carr & Co (1996), 197 AR 6 at para 17, 46 Alta LR (3d) 324 (QB) [Carr]. In Rath & Co. v. Sweetgrass First Nation, 2013 ABQB 165, 2013 CarswellAlta 399, 559 A.R. 12, 85 Alta. L.R. (5th) 219, Justice Tilleman gave the following summary of the law (at paragraphs 24–29): 24 Under the Old Rules, appeals of a taxing officer's decision were not a de novo hearing. Rather, deference was owed to the decisions made by a taxing officer. In McLennan Ross v. Keen Industries Ltd (No 2) (1988), 86 AR 311 at para 12 (CA) [McLennan Ross 2], the Alberta Court of Appeal said: There are practical grounds for not making the hearing before the reviewing judge a de novo hearing. In the first place, the taxing officer will often hear evidence and examine material which gives rise to questions of credit or weight. A chambers judge cannot effectively substitute his views on such questions. Moreover, the taxing officer's function is a specialized one and he may have to bring his own experience and expertise to bear. It is thus unlikely that the standard of review should be “de novo”. 25 At para 13, the Court of Appeal found: In my view in Alberta the primary question on review of a quantum fixed by a taxing officer is (as in many other jurisdictions) whether he has made an error of principle, or whether the award is inordinately high or low. 26 This rule was, and remains, consistently applied: Anderson v. Brink (BV) Professional Corp (1990), 107 AR 143 at para 2 (CA) [Ben Vanden], 509703 Alberta Ltd v. Witten Binder, 2000 ABQB 729 at para 19 [Witten Binder]. New rule 10.26(2) specifies that an appeal from a review officer's decision to this court is not de novo; it is an appeal on the record. After reviewing and confirming the deferential standard of review applicable to an appeal from a review officer's decision, Justice Yamauchi in FMC v. Kristof Financial Inc, 2012 ABQB 359 at para 18, 215 ACWS (3d) 1010 [FMC] stated “the parties must put forward their ‘best case’ to the review officer; not to the court hearing the appeal.” 27 A decision of a review officer should not be interfered with unless some improper principle was relied upon, the quantum of the reviewed account is so inordinately high or low as to reveal a mistaken principle, the review officer fails to consider the evidence and representations made before the officer, or a finding of fact is clearly in error: McLennan Ross v. Keen Industries Ltd (1987), 83 AR 322 at para 6 (CA) [McLennan Ross 1], McLennan Ross 2 at paras 6 and 13, Carr & Co v. Markdale Ltd (1996), 197 AR 6 at para 17 (QB) [Carr & Co], Pacholok v. Nichols (Neil W) Professional Corp (1991), 117 AR 300 at para 19 (CA), Pentz v. Salmon, [1996] A.J. No. 359, 1996 CarswellAlta 320 at para 5, [1996] AWLD 496 (CA), Witten Binder at para 19, FMC at para 17, Carter v. Blake (1982), 41 AR 418 at para 7 (NWT CA). These are reversible errors. 28 In ascertaining value, the courts have again held that the review officer employs a specialized expertise and is entitled to deference: Carr & Co at para 20, Morrison v. Pantony (Rod) Professional Corp, 2008 ABCA 145 at para 30, 429 AR 259 [Rod Pantony Corp], FMC at para 16. 29 But, where interference with a review officer's decision is justified, the Court may reassess the account itself or return it for a new assessment, among other possible remedies: McLennan Ross 2 at para 6, Ben Vanden at para 4, rule 10.27(1). 3. A Litigant in Dedicated Pursuit of Legal Rights As a last matter, I deal briefly with the contention made on behalf of the Appellant respecting the unreported bench decision of Harradence, J.A. for the Alberta Court of Appeal in Hanson v. McCormick. I cannot agree with the assertion of the Appellant that the decision stands for the proposition that when a litigant is in dedicated pursuit of his legal rights as a matter of principle, that litigant must generally take responsibility for the fees that emanate from that course of action. First of all, I am not satisfied that is what His Lordship was saying in Hanson. Secondly, I agree with the contention of counsel for the Respondent that bench decisions have little precedential value because they are often lacking in detail and can therefore not be evaluated adequately. Indeed, if one reads the very short decision in Hanson, one comes to the conclusion that none of the facts can be divined from the decision, which is scarcely more than a page long. Carr & Co. v. Markdale Ltd. (1996), 46 Alta. L.R. (3d) 324 (Q.B.), at 334, per Jones J.

Nature of Hearing The appeal is not a hearing de novo.

The majority of Canadian authorities support the conclusion that on an appeal from a taxing officer “the judicial approach appears rather uniform and is one of non-interference unless the taxing master operated on a wrong principle and thereby fell into error”.
This statement is taken from a judgment of the Nova Scotia Supreme Court Appeal Division in Cape Breton Landowners v.
Stora Kopparbergs Bergslags Aktiebolag (1983), 33 C.P.C.
1 … The relevant Nova Scotia rule is in the same terms as R.
A number of other authorities are review in that decision.
If the quantum awarded can be said to be inordinately high or low, that is a ground of interference because it betrays an error of principle.
Once error is found the reviewing court may then make its own assessment.
The solicitors cite Carter v.
418 (N.W.T.C.A.), where the comparable rule in the Northwest Territories was under consideration.
McClung J.A. speaks of the “de novo” aspect of the proceedings before him.
That case acknowledges that the judge hearing the appeal from a taxation may review a finding of fact that is clearly in error, although McClung J.A. upheld the taxing officer's fact finding.

The case does not decide whether the proceeding before the judge hearing an appeal from a taxing officer is de novo but it reaffirms the rule that fact findings by a taxing officer “should be treated with the same consideration and on the same footing as those made by a trial Judge”, citing Re Solicitor
C.A.) … The solicitors' case is based on the assumption that the calculation of the proper amount of fees is, itself, a matter of discretion.
While we do find that term used from time to time, I prefer the view that the assessment is not “the exercise of a discretion”.
It is a determination of value or worth which ordinarily involves a weighing of the factors relevant to that assessment like any determination of a quantum meruit claim.
I do not read R.
657 as giving the judge sitting on appeal a power to reassess or reweigh the material before the taxing officer.
There are some matters of discretion open to a taxing officer and open for review by the judge hearing the appeal, but not the assessment of a value.
In making his assessment the taxing officer is not exercising a discretion, any more than the judge who fixes general damages is exercising a discretion.
There are practical grounds for not making the hearing before the reviewing judge a de novo hearing.
In the first place, the taxing officer will often hear evidence and examine material which gives rise to questions of credit or weight.
A chambers judge cannot effectively substitute his views on such questions.
Moreover, the taxing officer's function is a specialized one and he may have to bring his own experience and expertise to bear.
It is thus unlikely that the standard of review should be “de novo”.

In my view in Alberta the primary question on review of a quantum fixed by a taxing officer is (as in many other jurisdictions) whether he has made an error of principle, or whether the award is inordinately high or low.

Mercantile Bank of Canada (1988), 59 Alta.

266 (Q.B.), Acton J. said (at pp.

Standard of Review The reasons of the taxing officer were, in our view, adequate.
This is not to say that his judgment cannot be questioned.

The correct standard of review in the circumstances to apply in circumstances of this case is whether the award of the taxing officer was so inordinately high or low as to require interference; the learned chambers judge did not apply that standard, and his decision cannot be left to stand.

Keen Industries Ltd.

Zavislake (1998), 215 A.R.

He or she may not substitute his or her opinion for that of the taxation officer, unless the award appears inordinately high or low, indicating an error of principle.
And Jones J. said at p.
333 of Carr & Co. v.
Markdale Ltd.
L.R.

(3d) 324 (Q.B.): It is clear from what the Court of Appeal had to say in the McLennan Ross cases that the Taxing Officer's decision can only be reversed if it is indicative of error in legal approach.

That error would likely appear only in one of two circumstances, namely, from either an enunciation of the application of a principle that would appear to be in error, or from the Taxing Officer having made an award that is either so inordinately high or so inordinately low that the Court must apprehend from the nature of the award that a wrong principle was applied.
The only other consideration that could have a bearing on matters would be whether the Taxing Officer had in fact considered the evidence and representations made before the officer.

Markdale Ltd., Mr.
Justice Jones noted that Taxing Officers acquire an expertise the benefits of which ought not to be lightly disregarded.
At pp.
333–34, his Lordship said: It should be noted that in the [Petty v.
Bishop (1977), 2 A.R.
241] case … Miller, J., at p.
244 … quotes from Frost v.
Frost, [1941] 3 W.W.R.

C.A.) at 274 where McDonald, J.A. said: The rule that a judge should not override a registrar (in matters of costs) except on a matter of principle has never been due to any jurisdictional restriction; it is simply a rule of policy and good sense, adopted because registrars can go into details better than can judges.
That is a major consideration in this case.
I have had the benefit of looking at the detailed accounts prepared and submitted by Carr & Company to the Taxing Officer.
I have read them and thought about them.

I am nevertheless at a disadvantage compared with the Taxing Officer whose duties commonly call for him to do this type of vetting because of the nature of his position and the expertise that he gathers in carrying out those duties.

Accordingly, I am not in a position to say, in the absence of any indication, that he followed a wrong principle or failed to follow an applicable principle, that he has erred in principle by the assessment which he has carried out.
Certainly, his enunciation of the various considerations that should go into consideration of the appropriateness of such fees is comprehensive and, in my respectful view, correct.

Nor can I conclude, in the circumstances of this case, that the reduction of $11,000, which he ordered, results in an award so inordinately low that it is reflective of the application of a wrong principle or principles.
Some deference is due to his determination because of his expertise and experience in this field.

266 (Q.B.), Acton J. said (at p.

Uned.
232, 2002 ABQB 158, sets out the standard for review of an appeal from a decision of a taxing officer.

Keen Industries Ltd.
(No.
311 (C.A), where Mr.
Justice Stevenson states (at para.

In my view, this Court sitting on appeal should not interfere with a finding of credibility unless there is a clear error of principle or law.

(1988), 86 AR 311 at para 7 (CA) [McLennan Ross 2]; 2. erring in principle

Sawridge Band, 2012 ABQB 44 at paras 36–37, 531 AR 158 [Twinn].
While it is important that decisions be fair, and efficient, finality also play a significant role in advancing the goals of review proceedings.

The content of the duty of fairness will also reflect the reality that, because of the nature of review proceedings, additional procedural protections are squared up against decisions made in a necessarily subjective area.

45 Ensuring a minimum standard of procedural fairness is reviewable on a correctness standard: Anderson at para 30. … 46 It is important that a person whose case is decided by a review officer has “a meaningful opportunity to present their case fully and fairly”: Baker at para 30 … … 51 … A review officer must consider the submissions of the parties at a review hearing: Carr & Co v.

Markdale Ltd (1996), 197 AR 6 at para 17 (QB). … 53 Where reasons are required, they should demonstrate “justification, transparency and intelligibility” in the decision-making process: Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses' Union v.
Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62 at para 1, [2011] 3 SCR 708 [Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses' Union].
54 A review officer is an expert decision maker and is presumed to know the principles applicable to a review proceeding.
Therefore, a review officer's reasons need not be extensive.
In Brown v.
Snyder & Associates, 2004 ABQB 899 at para 25, 364 A.R.

266, Acton J stated: [T]he case law is clear that taxing officers are not required to give extensive reasons … While a complete lack of reasons may be grounds to refer a matter back to the taxing officer, as found in Penonzek v.
Cerra, 2001 ABQB 272, any deficiencies in the articulation of the Taxing Officer's reasons in this case are not a sufficient basis for me to interfere with his decision.
[Citations omitted.] 55 Because of their nature, review awards are perhaps subject to the appearance of arbitrariness, although they may not actually be arbitrary or unfair.

Mathisen
(4th) 78 at para 22, 79 ACWS

(3d) 168 accepted “an element of arbitrariness” in the reviewed account because reviewing a lawyer's bill “is an assessment, not merely a mathematical exercise.” … 57 With reference to Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses' Union, the Alberta Court of Appeal recently wrote about the adequacy of reasons in Lameman v.
Alberta, 2013 ABCA 148 at para 57: In Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses' Union v.

Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62 at para 12, [2011] 3 SCR 708, the Supreme Court of Canada stated that a reviewing court is entitled to consider what reasons a decision-maker could have given.

First, the retainer agreement must be understood.

Morrow, 2004 ABCA 150 at para 11, 348 AR 118.

That rule lists a number of factors including “any other factor that is appropriate to consider in the circumstances.” Case law and the Law Society of Alberta, Code of Conduct [Code of Conduct] are sources that help identify other potentially relevant factors.
