Witten Binder, 2000 ABQB 729 at paras 27–30, McLennan Ross 1 at para 9; Morrison v.

Pantony (Rod) Professional Corp, 2008 ABCA 145 at para 26, 429 AR 259 [Rod Pantony Corp] Code of Conduct r 2.06(1) commentary factors (excluding those already listed) include: the time and effort required and spent; any special skill or service that has been required and provided; fees authorized by statute or regulation; special circumstances; the likelihood, if made known to the client, that acceptance of the retainer will result in the lawyer's inability to accept other employment; the experience and ability of the lawyer; any estimate or range of fees given by the lawyer; and the client's prior consent to the fee.
Repchuk v.
Silverberg, 2013 ABQB 305, was referred to with approval in Ashraf v.
Zinner Law Office, 2013 ABQB 730, 2013 CarswellAlta 2546, 578 A.R.
In Fraser Milner Casgrain LLP v.
Kristof Financial Inc., 2012 ABQB 359, 2012 CarswellAlta 954, 541 A.R.

245, Justice Yamauchi said, at paragraphs 16–18: 16 When one reviews the many cases that deal with appeals from decisions of review officers (or taxing officers, as they were formerly known), there are certain principles that emerge.
A review officer's decision is entitled to curial deference: 509703 at para 11.
Why?
A review officer's “duties commonly call for him to do this type of vetting because of the nature of his position and the expertise that he gathers in carrying out those duties”: Carr & Co v.
Markdale Ltd.
(1996), 46 Alta LR (3d) 324 at para 20 (QB) [“Carr & Company”].
See also McLennan Ross v.
Mercantile Bank of Canada (1988), 59 Alta LR (2d) 369 at para 6 (CA) [“McLennan Ross”].
The Alberta Court of Appeal in McLennan Ross went on to say that, “the taxing officer's function is a specialized one and he may have to bring his own experience and expertise to bear” (at para 12).
17 Curial deference, however, is not absolute.

A court hearing an appeal from a review officer's decision may interfere if the review officer “operated on a wrong principle and thereby fell into error”: McLennan Ross at para 6, citing Cape Breton Landowners v.
Stora Kopparbergs Bergslags Aktiebolag (1983), 33 CPC 1, 146 DLR (3d) 369, 58 NSR (2d) 193, 123 APR (NSCA); Petty v.
Bishop & McKenzie (1977), 2 AR 241 at 243 (QB).
An error in principle may include a situation where the quantum that the review officer awards is inordinately high or low: McLennan Ross ibid; 509703 at para 11.

Similarly, a court hearing an appeal from a review officer's decision may interfere if the review officer makes an error concerning the scope of the retainer agreement under which the parties are operating: Brown v.
Snyder & Associates, 2004 ABQB 899 at para 20 [“Brown”].
Finally, a court hearing an appeal from a review officer's decision may find that the review officer made a finding of fact that is clearly in error: Carter v.
Blake (1982), 41 AR 418 at para 7 (NWTCA) [“Carter”].

18 With respect to the latter point, a court hearing an appeal from a review officer's decision must exercise caution, and must not step too far into arena of gathering evidence and weighing that evidence.
As the court said in McLennan Ross at paras 11–12: I do not read R.
657 as giving the judge sitting on appeal a power to reassess or reweigh the material before the taxing officer.
There are some matters of discretion open to a taxing officer and open for review by the judge hearing the appeal, but not the assessment of a value.
In making his assessment the taxing officer is not exercising a discretion, any more than the judge who fixes general damages is exercising a discretion.
There are practical grounds for not making the hearing before the reviewing judge a de novo hearing.
In the first place, the taxing officer will often hear evidence and examine material which gives rise to questions of credit or weight.
A chambers judge cannot effectively substitute his views on such questions.
This makes it clear that the parties must put forward their “best case” to the review officer; not to the court hearing the appeal.
In Ashraf v.
Zinner Law Office, 2013 ABQB 730, 2013 CarswellAlta 2546, 578 A.R.

(7th) 145, Justice Sullivan referred with approval to those statements by Justice Yamauchi's, and added this comment (at paragraph 29): 29 Additionally, a review officer's decision may be interfered with if the review officer failed to consider the parties' evidence and representations made on the review: Sweetgrass First Nation v.
Rath & Company, 2013 ABQB 165 at para 27 [Rath]; Markdale Ltd v.
Carr & Co (1996), 197 AR 6 at para 17, 46 Alta LR (3d) 324 (QB) [Carr].
In Rath & Co. v.
Sweetgrass First Nation, 2013 ABQB 165, 2013 CarswellAlta 399, 559 A.R.
12, 85 Alta.
L.R.
(5th) 219, Justice Tilleman gave the following summary of the law (at paragraphs 24–29): 24 Under the Old Rules, appeals of a taxing officer's decision were not a de novo hearing.
Rather, deference was owed to the decisions made by a taxing officer.
In McLennan Ross v.

Keen Industries Ltd (No 2) (1988), 86 AR 311 at para 12 (CA) [McLennan Ross 2], the Alberta Court of Appeal said: There are practical grounds for not making the hearing before the reviewing judge a de novo hearing.
In the first place, the taxing officer will often hear evidence and examine material which gives rise to questions of credit or weight.
A chambers judge cannot effectively substitute his views on such questions.
Moreover, the taxing officer's function is a specialized one and he may have to bring his own experience and expertise to bear.
It is thus unlikely that the standard of review should be “de novo”.

25 At para 13, the Court of Appeal found: In my view in Alberta the primary question on review of a quantum fixed by a taxing officer is (as in many other jurisdictions) whether he has made an error of principle, or whether the award is inordinately high or low.
26 This rule was, and remains, consistently applied: Anderson v.
Brink (BV) Professional Corp (1990), 107 AR 143 at para 2 (CA) [Ben Vanden], 509703 Alberta Ltd v.
Witten Binder, 2000 ABQB 729 at para 19 [Witten Binder].
New rule 10.26(2) specifies that an appeal from a review officer's decision to this court is not de novo; it is an appeal on the record.
After reviewing and confirming the deferential standard of review applicable to an appeal from a review officer's decision, Justice Yamauchi in FMC v.
Kristof Financial Inc, 2012 ABQB 359 at para 18, 215 ACWS

(3d) 1010 [FMC] stated “the parties must put forward their ‘best case’ to the review officer; not to the court hearing the appeal.” 27 A decision of a review officer should not be interfered with unless some improper principle was relied upon, the quantum of the reviewed account is so inordinately high or low as to reveal a mistaken principle, the review officer fails to consider the evidence and representations made before the officer, or a finding of fact is clearly in error: McLennan Ross v.
Keen Industries Ltd (1987), 83 AR 322 at para 6 (CA) [McLennan Ross 1], McLennan Ross 2 at paras 6 and 13, Carr & Co v.
Markdale Ltd (1996), 197 AR 6 at para 17 (QB) [Carr & Co], Pacholok v.
Nichols (Neil W) Professional Corp (1991), 117 AR 300 at para 19 (CA), Pentz v.
Salmon, [1996] A.J.
No.
359, 1996 CarswellAlta 320 at para 5, [1996] AWLD 496 (CA), Witten Binder at para 19, FMC at para 17, Carter v.
Blake (1982), 41 AR 418 at para 7 (NWT CA).
These are reversible errors.
28 In ascertaining value, the courts have again held that the review officer employs a specialized expertise and is entitled to deference: Carr & Co at para 20, Morrison v.
Pantony (Rod) Professional Corp, 2008 ABCA 145 at para 30, 429 AR 259 [Rod Pantony Corp], FMC at para 16.

29 But, where interference with a review officer's decision is justified, the Court may reassess the account itself or return it for a new assessment, among other possible remedies: McLennan Ross 2 at para 6, Ben Vanden at para 4, rule 10.27(1).

A Litigant in Dedicated Pursuit of Legal Rights As a last matter, I deal briefly with the contention made on behalf of the Appellant respecting the unreported bench decision of Harradence, J.A. for the Alberta Court of Appeal in Hanson v.
McCormick.

I cannot agree with the assertion of the Appellant that the decision stands for the proposition that when a litigant is in dedicated pursuit of his legal rights as a matter of principle, that litigant must generally take responsibility for the fees that emanate from that course of action.
First of all, I am not satisfied that is what His Lordship was saying in Hanson.

Secondly, I agree with the contention of counsel for the Respondent that bench decisions have little precedential value because they are often lacking in detail and can therefore not be evaluated adequately.
Indeed, if one reads the very short decision in Hanson, one comes to the conclusion that none of the facts can be divined from the decision, which is scarcely more than a page long.
Carr & Co. v.
Markdale Ltd.
L.R.
(3d) 324 (Q.B.), at 334, per Jones J.

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 10.29 – Part 10. Lawyers' Charges, Recoverable Costs Of Litigation, And Sanctions
paragraphs.text: (1) A successful party to an application, a proceeding or an action is entitled to a costs award against the unsuccessful party, and the unsuccessful party must pay the costs forthwith, notwithstanding the final determination of the application, proceeding or action, subject to (a) the Court's general discretion under rule 10.31, (b) the assessment officer's discretion under rule 10.41, (c) particular rules governing who is to pay costs in particular circumstances, (d) an enactment governing who is to pay costs in particular circumstances, and (e) subrule (2). (2) If an application or proceeding is heard without notice to a party, the Court may (a) make a costs award with respect to the application or proceeding, or (b) defer making a decision on who is liable to pay the costs of the application or proceeding until every party is served with notice of the date, time and place at which the Court will consider who is liable to pay the costs.
